title: ADHD in Women: Why It Gets Missed for Decades
description:
ADHD in women looks completely different from the textbook version, and that difference is exactly why so many women go undiagnosed until their 30s, 40s, or even later. This video breaks down the real neuroscience behind why female ADHD is so often mistaken for anxiety, laziness, or just 'being a lot', and what the symptoms actually look like in daily life. We cover the hormonal connection, the masking that exhausts you from the inside out, and what to do if you finally see yourself in this. If you have ever been told you are too sensitive, too scattered, or not sick enough to have ADHD, this one is for you.

chapters.title: The Diagnosis That Never Came
chapters.voiceover: You were the girl who got good grades but cried in the bathroom before every test. The one who could read the same paragraph six times and still have no idea what it said. You were called sensitive, spacey, dramatic, a dreamer. Teachers said you were smart but not working to your potential. Your mum said you just needed to try harder. And somehow, despite all of it, you kept functioning. You kept showing up. So nobody called it anything. Nobody called it ADHD. Here is the thing that most people do not know: the entire framework we use to identify ADHD was built almost exclusively on research done on young boys. Hyperactive boys. Disruptive boys. Boys whose symptoms were impossible to ignore in a classroom. Girls were not in those studies in any meaningful numbers, which means the diagnostic checklist was never really built with girls in mind. So when a girl with ADHD sat quietly, stared out the window, handed in perfect work that took her four times longer than everyone else, she did not get flagged. She got overlooked. Fast forward twenty or thirty years, and that girl is now a woman sitting in a doctor's office for the first time, holding a list of symptoms she printed from the internet, wondering if she is allowed to be here. This video is for her. We are going to cover what ADHD actually looks like in women, why it gets missed, what the science says, and what you can do about it. Stay with me.

chapters.title: What It Actually Looks Like
chapters.voiceover: When people think ADHD, they picture a kid bouncing off the walls. What they do not picture is a thirty-four-year-old woman who has had an email open on her screen for forty minutes and still cannot start typing the reply. It is Tuesday morning. The email is not even complicated. She knows what she wants to say. But there is this wall between knowing and doing, and she cannot explain it, and she hates herself a little more each time the cursor blinks. That is ADHD. Not hyperactivity in the physical sense, but a nervous system that struggles to initiate, to transition, to regulate its own attention. In women, ADHD most commonly presents as the inattentive subtype. That means the loudest symptoms are internal: racing thoughts that never quiet down, extreme difficulty starting tasks that feel low-interest even when the stakes are high, losing track of time so consistently that it feels like a personality flaw, emotional responses that are intense and fast and hard to pull back from. There is also rejection sensitive dysphoria, which is not in the official diagnostic criteria but is reported by a huge proportion of ADHD women. It is the specific, searing pain of feeling criticised or left out, a pain that is neurologically disproportionate to the event but feels completely real in the body. And then there is the chronic overwhelm of a to-do list that lives in your head because writing it down somehow makes it worse. The clutter that spreads because starting to tidy requires the same executive resources that are already depleted. The appointments forgotten not because you do not care, but because your brain does not maintain information passively the way other brains do. This is not a character flaw. This is a dopamine regulation problem, and we need to talk about what that actually means.

chapters.title: The Neuroscience (Simply Put)
chapters.voiceover: Let us talk about what is actually happening in there, because understanding the mechanism is one of the most relieving things you can do. ADHD is fundamentally a disorder of dopamine regulation. Dopamine is not just the reward chemical people talk about. In the prefrontal cortex, the part of your brain that handles planning, prioritising, starting tasks, and regulating emotions, dopamine acts more like a signal stabiliser. It helps neurons hold on to the information they need long enough to act on it. In the ADHD brain, dopamine transmission in the prefrontal cortex is less efficient. The signal is weaker and less consistent. What this means in practice is that the prefrontal cortex struggles to do its job: it cannot easily hold a goal in working memory while also managing the steps required to reach it. It cannot reliably apply the brakes to an emotional response before it spills out. It cannot generate the internal motivation to start something just because it is important. Instead, the ADHD brain is heavily dependent on what researchers call interest-based motivation. Tasks get done when they are novel, urgent, personally meaningful, or when someone else is present to create accountability. This is not a choice. It is the difference between a brain that can manufacture motivation and one that needs to find it externally. Norepinephrine also plays a role here, affecting alertness and arousal regulation, which is why focus can be so inconsistent. Hyperfocus is part of this too: when interest is high enough, dopamine transmission temporarily normalises and the brain locks in, sometimes for hours. That is not proof that you can focus when you try. It is proof that the system works when the neurochemical conditions are right. Understanding this reframes everything. You are not lazy. Your brain is running a different operating system.

chapters.title: Masking: The Hidden Exhaustion
chapters.voiceover: Here is the part that breaks my heart a little, because it is so common and so invisible. Masking is what happens when you spend years learning to hide your symptoms so thoroughly that even the people closest to you do not know anything is wrong. And often, you do not fully know either. For women with ADHD, masking starts early. You watch how other people manage things and you reverse-engineer the behaviour. You make to-do lists not because they help you but because that is what organised people do. You over-explain yourself in emails to compensate for the anxiety of not being sure if you are making sense. You arrive early to avoid the shame spiral of being late, burning enormous energy on logistics that other people just handle automatically. You script conversations in advance. You stay quiet in meetings because you know your thoughts are coming out in the wrong order and you need more time to sort them. From the outside, all of this looks like competence. It looks like a woman who has it together. Inside, it is absolutely exhausting. Masking works well enough to fool diagnostic tools, which is a major reason women get missed. Clinicians see a woman who makes eye contact, communicates clearly, holds a job, and they do not see ADHD. They see anxiety, maybe depression, maybe just stress. And the woman herself often does not push back because she has spent her whole life being told she is fine, so she has internalised that version of herself. The cost of masking is not just tiredness. Research links chronic masking to significantly higher rates of anxiety, depression, and burnout in women with ADHD compared to men. When you spend your entire cognitive budget on appearing neurotypical, there is nothing left over for actually living.

chapters.title: Hormones and the Cycle Nobody Talks About
chapters.voiceover: There is one piece of the female ADHD picture that almost never comes up, and it is genuinely important. Oestrogen has a direct effect on dopamine transmission. Higher oestrogen levels, which happen in the first half of the menstrual cycle and during pregnancy, can temporarily improve dopamine signalling in the prefrontal cortex. Some women with ADHD report that the week after their period ends is their best week, mentally. They can start things. They can follow through. They feel almost like a different person. Then oestrogen drops in the second half of the cycle, particularly in the week before menstruation, and the floor falls out. Focus collapses, emotional regulation becomes nearly impossible, the executive function that was barely adequate becomes completely unreliable. This is not PMS in the casual sense. This is a real neurochemical shift that hits harder for ADHD brains because those brains were already working closer to the edge of their dopamine capacity. This pattern also explains why perimenopause is a crisis point for so many undiagnosed women. As oestrogen declines in the years approaching menopause, the coping strategies that have worked for decades suddenly stop working. Women who managed reasonably well at thirty-five find themselves at forty-five completely overwhelmed by things that used to be hard but manageable. This is when many women finally get diagnosed, not because their ADHD got worse, but because the hormonal scaffolding that was quietly helping them compensate has been removed. If you are in that window and things feel like they are falling apart, please know that this is a documented, biological process, and there is support available. Tracking your cycle alongside your ADHD symptoms, even just in a notes app, can give you and any clinician you see genuinely useful data.

chapters.title: Where to Go From Here
chapters.voiceover: If you have watched this far and something in you has gone quiet and still in a way that is unfamiliar, that recognition matters. It is not a diagnosis, but it is information, and information is where everything starts. Here is what actually helps, practically and concretely. First: if you are seeking a diagnosis, go in prepared. Document specific examples, not just feelings. Not 'I have trouble focusing', but 'on three occasions this week I sat down to work and could not begin a task for over an hour despite wanting to'. Specificity matters because clinicians need to see impairment, not just traits. Second: the strategies that help neurotypical people organise themselves often fail ADHD brains because they require consistent self-initiation, which is exactly the thing that is impaired. What works better is reducing the number of decisions required. Body doubling, working alongside someone else virtually or in person, borrows their dopamine without requiring any extra effort from you. Externalising your working memory, which means putting everything outside your head into a visible system, removes the cognitive load of trying to hold it all internally. Time blocking with built-in transition buffers accounts for the fact that switching tasks is genuinely costly for an ADHD brain. Third: medication is not a moral choice. For many women with ADHD, stimulant or non-stimulant medication is the most evidence-based intervention available. It does not change who you are. It adjusts the neurochemical conditions so that the capable, creative, deeply feeling person you already are can actually function. And finally: the years you spent not knowing were not wasted. They built something in you, a resilience and an adaptability that is real. The diagnosis is not the end of a story. It is the first page of one where you finally have the right information. Follow for daily ADHD content, because there is so much more to cover and you deserve to understand your own brain.
